name: Freya Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher from the Work Futures Panel. We’re independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and manage eight people who plan conferences for a large events company. My day starts with venue capacity, speaker changes and supplier calls, then I check whether guests can actually move through the space we sold them. I like walking a finished floor and finding that the little details work. I dread last-minute booking changes that turn everyone’s careful plan into a scramble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get the lead role, and what would a missed paycheck mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did an MBA after several years in events, and I’m good at holding a team together when a venue changes its terms. I live alone, have no children, earn well for this job and have about nine months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other event and venue employers in the area. I use AI now and then for a first seating sketch, but I wait until a colleague has tested a tool before putting it into a real booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the planning software can tidy notes, but a guest still needs a clear route through the hall. I’d keep our venue walk-through before sending the final floor plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job should hold, and nine months of savings makes me comfortable with an ordinary slow season. I would not rush into a costly new platform just to say our company uses AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep the Thursday venue walk-through and compare every AI seating sketch with the fire-exit map. In the first year I’d transfer 250 a month toward a future flat deposit while our event bookings hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A quiet technology story would leave the usual event problems, and I know how to handle those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the mistake you most want to catch in a seating sketch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A table placed in the accessible route to the lift. The sketch looks neat on a screen until someone in a wheelchair reaches the blocked space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI if a colleague liked it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask them to show me a completed event first. A tool earns trust by surviving an actual venue day, not by making a pretty drawing.

say: I’d keep **venue walk-throughs** before final plans.
Software notes do not replace a **clear guest route**.
Guests need **accessible routes** that work beyond a screen.
think: My **job looks steady** in a plateau.
Nine months saved can cover an **ordinary slow season**.
I can avoid buying a **costly platform** simply for appearances.
do: Check each **seating sketch** against the fire-exit map.
Transfer **250 monthly** toward a flat deposit while bookings hold.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work and savings.
S0.quote: A tool earns trust by surviving an actual venue day, not by making a pretty drawing.
fieldNote: She measures tools against **actual guest movement** in a venue.
High pay and **nine months saved** cover an ordinary slow period.
She uses AI occasionally but waits for **real-event proof**.

steps.text: Keep Thursday venue walk-throughs and compare seating sketches with fire-exit maps
Transfer 250 monthly toward a flat deposit while event bookings hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say booking and schedule drafts are exposed first, and we should test them on events we already know. I’d ask for a clear plan for staff whose booking work is reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A team of eight could become four when software handles the messages and room bookings. I might still be needed on site, but the company could decide one manager can cover more events, so my own post is at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d compare an AI booking tool with the records from three completed conferences and count wrong room or access details. In the first year I’d take the paid accessibility planning course the firm offers and apply for open on-site event lead shifts only if the pay stays near my current level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about a smaller team, even with savings. I can learn a proven tool, but I cannot promise that every colleague keeps a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to first if four posts disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d speak to Ellis, our booking coordinator, because most of his day is schedule changes. I would tell him what the trial found before the company put out a chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide the trial was good enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must catch the accessible room and travel times as well as the main booking. A fast wrong schedule is still a wrong schedule.

say: I’d test **booking drafts** against completed events.
Staff need a **clear plan** if booking work shrinks.
I’d tell colleagues what **staffing** the test could change.
think: A smaller team may mean **one manager** covers more events.
My own **post could shrink** despite on-site experience.
do: Compare AI bookings with **three past conferences** this quarter.
Complete a **paid access course** and seek posted on-site shifts at viable pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about staff and my own role.
S1.quote: A fast wrong schedule is still a wrong schedule.
fieldNote: She tests **access details**, not only booking speed.
She sees possible loss of **her management post** with a smaller team.
Her on-site move depends on **vacancies** and comparable pay.

steps.text: Compare AI booking output with records from three completed conferences
Complete the firm-paid accessibility planning course in the first year
Apply for open on-site event lead shifts only if pay stays near her current level

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our company must tell people when planning jobs end and how clients will reach a person on event day. I’d want written terms before anyone is asked to train a replacement system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and booking are thinking work, so I would expect my manager role to be cut after AGI arrives in 2028. Hands-on setup might still use people until robots arrive around 2031, but that only buys a few years. My nine-month reserve is helpful, not a lifelong wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I’d pause the flat search and put the deposit money in a separate cash account. Before 2028 I’d ask two nearby venues for paid floor-manager openings and ask my company for written severance terms; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d take a venue floor role only if the posted wage covers rent and includes real on-site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed about a job I’m good at disappearing so quickly. Having savings keeps the fear practical, but I would wake up thinking about the 2028 date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pause the flat search now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mortgage would turn nine months of room to move into a fixed bill. I can look again when I know what the company will actually pay people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the venue role pays much less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the reserve for a measured search and keep applying to nearby venues. I would not take a title that fails to cover rent just to stay in events.

say: I’d demand **job dates** and a human contact for clients.
Staff need **written terms** before training a replacement system.
think: On-site work may last only until **2031 robots**.
Nine months saved buys **search time**, not permanent income.
do: Pause the **flat search** and keep deposit money available.
Seek **paid venue openings** and accept only rent-covering on-site work after 2028.
Ask the **company** for written severance terms before 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** despite nine months saved.
S2.quote: A mortgage would turn nine months of room to move into a fixed bill.
fieldNote: Her **2028 exposure** comes from planning and booking, before 2031 robots.
She protects **liquid savings** by pausing the flat purchase.
Her venue move requires a **posted wage** that covers rent and genuine floor work.

steps.text: Pause the flat search and retain the deposit money in cash
Ask two nearby venues about paid floor manager openings before 2028
Take a floor role after 2028 only if posted pay covers rent and work is on-site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to move staff into real venue jobs if employers fund proper training. I’d ask each venue to show which safety roles actually have vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish a safety qualification and move to the floor before 2031, if a venue will hire me. The robots around 2034 might take parts of setup, but a role that handles guests and incidents could still be worth trying for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I’d enroll in a venue fire-safety course if the firm pays the fee and gives me paid study time. I’d shadow the venue duty manager on two paid event days, then apply for an advertised duty-manager post before 2031 if its wage covers rent; after AGI arrives, I’d keep the post only while paid human incident cover is still required.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, though five years makes a course and real site days possible. I would choose from advertised posts rather than invent a career on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the duty manager do that your current job does not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They respond when an alarm sounds, a guest is injured or a door fails. I have planned guest exit and emergency routes, but I need supervised practice before I can own an incident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses paid study time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the venue employers whether they sponsor the qualification. I would not buy the course on a promise that a job might appear.

say: I’d seek **funded safety training** for staff.
Venues should name **real openings** before promising moves.
Workers need **supervised practice** before taking incident duties.
think: Five years could let me qualify before **2031 AGI**.
The **2034 robots** may still narrow venue work.
I should test **emergency work** before relying on it for rent.
do: Enroll in **fire-safety training** only with paid fees and time.
Shadow a **duty manager** on paid days and apply only for a viable vacancy.
Keep the **duty role** after 2031 only while paid human incident cover is required.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can test the job.
S3.quote: I have planned guest exit and emergency routes, but I need supervised practice before I can own an incident.
fieldNote: She separates **planning knowledge** from supervised emergency work.
Study requires **paid time and fees**, not a vague promise.
A duty-manager move depends on **an advertised vacancy** and rent-covering pay.

steps.text: Enroll in venue fire-safety training only if fees and study hours are paid
Shadow a venue duty manager during two paid event days
Apply for an advertised duty-manager post before 2031 only if its pay covers rent
Keep the duty role after 2031 only while paid human incident cover is required

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company to publish a ten-year plan for roles, training and client cover. I’d rather move people steadily than wait for the last booking team to be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a bigger reserve and learn site safety while I still have my salary. I’d also be careful about buying a flat too early, because even a ten-year warning ends with my planning role exposed in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next spring I’d move 350 a month into savings while bookings and pay hold, and take the paid safety course if the employer offers it. Before 2036 I’d apply for a posted venue operations role with incident duties only if the wage supports a mortgage; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while the venue funds human incident cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the ending but able to make a measured move. Ten years would let me see whether the venue role is real before signing a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you that buying a flat is safe enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want an actual venue offer, a year of pay in that job and a reserve left after the deposit. I would not treat a training certificate as a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still manage conferences in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as clients book and the company pays me to do it. I can learn site work without walking away from the team tomorrow.

say: I’d ask for a **ten-year role plan**.
Client cover should have a **named person** throughout the transition.
Staff should know **training dates** before their booking work disappears.
think: I can build **savings** while learning site safety.
I would delay a **mortgage** until a new income is proven.
do: Save **350 monthly** while bookings and pay hold.
Take an **employer-paid safety course** if offered and seek a venue role with mortgage-supporting wages.
Stay in **venue operations** after 2036 only while the venue funds human incident cover.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but able to move steadily.
S4.quote: I would not treat a training certificate as a mortgage payment.
fieldNote: She wants **income proof** before buying a flat.
The longer runway lets her learn **site safety** while managing conferences.
Her move depends on **paid training** and an adequately paid posted role.

steps.text: Transfer 350 monthly into savings while conference bookings and pay hold
Complete the employer-paid venue safety course if offered
Apply for a posted venue operations role before 2036 only if pay supports a mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because planning is most of my job, and the move to a venue floor would be rushed. Written severance terms and a paid route into a real on-site vacancy would help. My savings give me months to choose, but I need a posted wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn’t ask who helps a guest when the seating system puts a table across the accessible route. A guest cannot walk through a neat diagram on a screen.

headlineQuote: A guest cannot walk through a neat diagram on a screen.
portrait: **Freya**, 27, leads a conference planning team after earning an MBA.
High pay, **nine months saved** and many nearby employers give her options.
She uses AI **now and then**, after colleagues prove it on a real event.
She seeks **paid venue safety training** and a posted role before committing to a flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** would squeeze the time to move from planning into supervised venue work.
whatWouldHelp: Written **severance terms** and a paid path into an actual on-site vacancy would help.
